title: Origins of Faceted Anomalous Scaling
authors: Maximilien Bernard, José Luis Iguain, Alejandro Kolton, Alberto Rosso
abstract: Fluctuating interfaces are typically characterized by their global, spectral, and local roughness exponents. Faceted anomalous scaling, characterized by $α_s>1$, $α_s\neqα$, and $α_{\mathrm{loc}}=1$, owes its name to the tendency of such interfaces to develop long, nearly linear segments called facets. Its statistical origin, and whether facets are required, have remained unclear. We show that this exponent structure is determined by the spatial statistics of the slope field. Slope increments split into typical fluctuations and rare, larger jumps. This anomalous scaling arises either when the typical slope increment displays genuine system-size-dependent anomalous scaling or when the rare jumps dominate the second moment. The two contributions can coexist, and their competition leads to bifractal scaling of the slopes. We establish this framework analytically in the generalized anharmonic Larkin model and the columnar Kardar--Parisi--Zhang equation, and we derive exactly the global, spectral, and local roughness exponents in both cases. The Larkin model realizes both mechanisms and produces anomalous interfaces with or without facets, whereas columnar KPZ belongs to the jump-dominated case and yields $α_s=3/2$.
summary: This work provides a rigorous statistical mechanical framework to understand 'faceted anomalous scaling' in fluctuating interfaces by analyzing the statistics of the slope field. It shows that the scaling exponents are determined by the competition between typical fluctuations and rare, large jumps in the slope increments. The analysis uses the Larkin and KPZ models to derive exact exponents, clarifying the physical conditions required for faceted versus non-faceted interface behavior.
main_problem:
The paper investigates the statistical origin of 'faceted anomalous scaling' in fluctuating interfaces, characterized by specific roughness exponents ($\alpha_s > 1, \alpha_s 
eq \alpha, \alpha_{	ext{loc}} = 1$). It seeks to determine whether this scaling is due to typical fluctuations or rare, large jumps in the slope field.
main_result: The anomalous scaling arises from the competition between typical and rare slope increments, which can be analytically derived in the generalized anharmonic Larkin model and the columnar KPZ equation. The columnar KPZ model, representing the rare-jump dominated case, yields specific exponents like $(\alpha, \alpha_s, \alpha_{	ext{loc}}) = (1, 3/2, 1)$.
method: The analysis involves decomposing the second moment of slope increments into typical and rare contributions, employing techniques like Brownian mapping, and analyzing the scaling behavior of the structure factor $S_h(k, L)$.
model_or_system: The study focuses on fluctuating interfaces modeled by the generalized anharmonic Larkin model and the columnar Kardar–Parisi–Zhang (KPZ) equation. These models describe the evolution of the interface height $h(x, t)$ under the influence of noise and non-linear slope terms.
key_observables: Global ($\alpha$), spectral ($\alpha_s$), and local ($\alpha_{	ext{loc}}$) roughness exponents; the structure factor $S_h(k, L)$; and the density of slope flips $ho_{	ext{flip}}(t, L)$.
important_parameters: The exponent $p$ governing the slope field statistics, which dictates the dominance of typical versus rare fluctuations; and the system size $L$ and time $t$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on decomposing the second moment of slope increments into typical and rare contributions, and uses approximations like linearizing the exact expression for slope increments in the Larkin model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the classification of scaling regimes based on slope field statistics, show the structure factor decay for columnar KPZ (exhibiting $k^{-4}$ and $k^{-2}$ decays), and track the time evolution of localized structures and the decay of slope flips.
paper_structure: The paper first defines the problem via roughness exponents, then analyzes the slope field statistics by splitting increments into typical and rare parts. It establishes the framework analytically using the Larkin model and the columnar KPZ equation, deriving specific exponent values for different physical limits.
why_interesting: The detailed mathematical framework connecting interface morphology (faceting) directly to the underlying statistical properties of the slope field is highly relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in complex systems, which shares mathematical structures with quantum many-body localization problems.
